remaining actions?
* * *
Suppose, that, in a case like our railroad case, the first injured passenger to sue loses his action against the railroad. The railroad cannot
plead that judgment against the next passenger to sue, because the second passenger was not a party to the first action, nor in privity with
the first passenger. Nevertheless, let us say that the second passenger also loses, and indeed that twenty-five passengers, in twenty-five
separate actions, all fail to establish negligence on the part of the railroad. Then passenger No. 26 wins his action. Are we to understand that
the remaining twenty-four passengers can plead the judgment in the case of No. 26 as conclusively establishing that the railroad was guilty
of negligence, while the railroad can make no reference to the first twenty-five cases which it won?
There is only one possible answer to this question: no such absurdity would be tolerated for a moment. The indefensibility of such a result
seems obvious * * *.
* * *
Our aversion to the twenty-sixth judgment as a conclusive adjudication stems largely from the feeling that such a judgment in such a series
must be an aberration, but we have no warrant for assuming that the aberrational judgment will not come as the first in the series.

3.What if before a case settles it yields a judicial finding that conflicts with a prior adjudication of the same issue? Such a finding could result, for
example, when a motion to dismiss is denied before a settlement is reached. Does that finding create sufficient inconsistency to block offensive issue
preclusion? In JACK FAUCETT ASSOCS. v. AMERICAN TELEPHONE & TELEGRAPH CO., 744 F.2d 118 (D.C.Cir. 1984), cert. denied, 469
U.S. 1196, 105 S.Ct. 980, 83 L.Ed.2d 982 (1985), Judge Mikva wrote for the court: “Parklane Hosiery does not hold that only inconsistent final

judgments can preclude offensive estoppel.” Id. at 130. Rather, according to Judge Mikva, the issue was whether “the inconsistency undermines the
court’s confidence in the correctness of the prior decision.” Id.
